site.claim: Your community, your node, your keys.
site.description: {brand} is an open-source community chat with end-to-end encryption, voice and video, and federation. Anyone can run a node; all nodes together form one network without a centre.

hero.title: Your community, your node, your keys.
hero.lead: {brand} is a chat for communities: text, voice and video, files, roles and moderation. Conversations are end-to-end encrypted, and anyone can run a node. All nodes together form one network, without a central service.
hero.status: {brand} is in private review; the first public release is coming soon.
features.title: What makes it different
features.lead: Everything a community needs to talk, built so that nobody in the middle can read along.
features.e2ee.title: Encrypted by default
features.e2ee.text: Channels, direct messages, attachments and calls are end-to-end encrypted. The keys stay on your devices, so the people who run a node cannot read your conversations.
features.federation.title: No centre
features.federation.text: Anyone can run a node, and all nodes form one network. With an account on one node you can join rooms on every other node. You can use your own domain for your address.
features.voice.title: Voice, video and screen sharing
features.voice.text: Talk, turn on your camera or share your screen. Calls are encrypted with keys from the same groups that protect the text.
features.bots.title: Bots that respect encryption
features.bots.text: A bot is a visible member with a badge, and everyone is told when it joins. Rooms can say "no bots", and webhooks can post into encrypted channels without being able to read them.
features.moderation.title: Moderation for real communities
features.moderation.text: Roles and permissions, an audit log, reports, bulk actions with a preview, and automatic moderation that works without reading encrypted messages.
features.selfhost.title: One container to self-host
features.selfhost.text: A node is one container image with the web app built in. Add a database and the reverse proxy you already have, and your community has its own home.
how.title: How it works
how.lead: Three ideas, and no central server anywhere.
how.home.title: Your account lives on your home node
how.home.text: You sign up on one node, your home node. Your address carries its domain, much like an e-mail address: alice@example.org.
how.room.title: A room lives on exactly one node
how.room.text: Each room lives on one node. Members from other nodes connect to it directly, so the room's data stays in one place instead of being copied everywhere.
how.notify.title: Nodes only pass on short notes
how.notify.text: Nodes send each other small signed notifications: an invite, a friend request, "you have a new message". The conversations themselves stay where they belong.
fed.heading: Interactive diagram: three nodes
fed.svg_title: Three nodes: example.org, Alice's home node; gaming.example, the node of the room night-owls; club.example, Ben's home node.
fed.text_home: Alice's account lives on her home node, example.org. That is where she signs in, and her address is alice@example.org.
fed.text_room: The room night-owls lives on exactly one node, gaming.example. Alice and Ben connect to it directly, each with a short-lived pass from their own home node.
fed.text_notify: Alice invites Ben. Her node sends a small signed note to Ben's home node, club.example. That kind of note is all nodes say to each other.
e2ee.title: What the node operator sees
e2ee.lead: End-to-end encryption means a message is locked on your device and only unlocked on the devices of the people in the conversation. The node in between stores and forwards it, but cannot read it.
e2ee.honest: To be honest about the limits: a node still sees metadata, such as who is in a room and when someone writes. Room admins can make a single channel readable on purpose, for example a large public one; then every app shows a permanent notice.
e2ee.msg2: I'm in. Bringing snacks for the stream.
e2ee.msg3: Same here. Voice opens at quarter to nine.
e2ee.sealed_sr: Encrypted message, unreadable without the keys.
e2ee.status_members: The members' devices hold the keys, so they read the messages as usual.
e2ee.status_node: The node only stores sealed messages. Without the keys, they are noise.
tour.title: A closer look
tour.lead: The web app works on phones, tablets and computers. Desktop and mobile apps are next.
tour.chat.title: Text channels
tour.chat.text: Formatting, code blocks, replies, reactions, pins and the member list, grouped by roles.
tour.voice.title: Voice and video
tour.voice.text: A stage for the people talking, cameras and screen sharing. Calls are end-to-end encrypted, too.
tour.files.title: Shared folders
tour.files.text: A folder tree per channel for the files a community keeps. Files channels are not end-to-end encrypted, and the app says so all the time.
tour.moderation.title: Roles and permissions
tour.moderation.text: Roles with plain switches for every permission, overrides per channel, an audit log and reports.
tour.search.title: Search
tour.search.text: Search works in encrypted channels as well: the index is built and kept on your own device.
selfhost.title: Run your own node
selfhost.lead: A {brand} node is one container image. Put it next to PostgreSQL and the reverse proxy you already have, set a few environment variables, and start it.
selfhost.needs: You need a domain, a server with Docker and, for voice, a range of open UDP ports. The first account becomes the node's admin.
selfhost.code_label: Starting a node with Docker Compose
selfhost.code_comment1: in a folder with the files from tavrn-node/deploy
selfhost.code_caption: The install guide walks through every step, including the reverse proxy and voice.
cta.title: Ready when you are
cta.lead: Open the web app in your browser, download the desktop app, or read how everything works.
cta.honest: {brand} is before its first public release, and the encryption has not been independently audited yet. Treat it as pre-release software for now.
download.title: Download
download.lead: Get {brand} for your computer, use it in the browser, or run your own node.
download.example_text: {brand} is in private review; the first public release is coming soon. The buttons switch on with it. Until then, version numbers, file names and sizes on this page are examples.
download.windows.title: Windows
download.windows.alt_summary: Problems with the standard app? Alternative build (Electron)
download.windows.alt_text: The standard app uses the WebView2 component of Windows. If it does not start or shows a blank window on your computer, this larger build brings its own browser engine instead.
download.linux.title: Linux
download.linux.electron: Built with Electron. Make the AppImage executable before you start it; the .deb package also adds the app to your menu.
download.macos.title: macOS
download.macos.later: A macOS app is planned. Until then, the web app works in Safari and every other current browser.
download.mobile.title: Android and iOS
download.mobile.later: Mobile apps are planned. Until then, the web app works in the browser of your phone; add it to your home screen for an app-like window.
download.verify.checksum_intro: Compare the SHA-256 checksum of the file you downloaded with the one listed here. If they differ, do not open the file.
download.verify.checksum_missing: The checksum is listed here once the release is published.
download.verify.how_windows: In PowerShell, in the folder of the download:
download.verify.how_linux: In a terminal, in the folder of the download:
download.verify.how_macos: In Terminal, in the folder of the download:
download.verify.how_android: On a computer, before you copy the file to your phone:
download.verify.signature: The .sig files next to the installers are signatures for the built-in updater: before the app installs an update, it checks the signature against the project's public key. You do not need them for a download by hand.
download.verify.electron_feed_linux: The Linux app updates itself from latest-linux.yml in the same release, which lists the SHA-512 of each package; the app checks that value before it installs an update.
download.verify.electron_feed_windows: The alternative Electron build updates itself from latest.yml in the same release and checks the SHA-512 listed there before it installs an update.
download.verify.unsigned_windows: The installers are not code-signed yet. Windows SmartScreen may warn that it "protected your PC" from an unrecognised app. After checking the checksum, choose "More info" and then "Run anyway".
download.verify.unsigned_linux: The packages are not signed with a package key yet, so your package manager cannot check them for you; the checksum is the check. Make an AppImage executable before starting it:
download.verify.unsigned_macos: The app is not notarised by Apple yet. macOS may say it cannot check the app for malicious software. After checking the checksum, open it from System Settings, Privacy & Security, "Open Anyway".
download.verify.unsigned_android: The app is not from an app store yet. Android asks you to allow installing apps from this source; allow it only for this file.

download.verifier.title: Check a downloaded file
download.verifier.lead: Choose the file you downloaded, and this page computes its checksum and compares it with the published ones.
download.verifier.private: The file is checked on your device and never uploaded.
download.verifier.expected_hint: Paste a SHA-256 or SHA-512 from the release page, as hex or base64.
download.verifier.nojs: Checking a file on this page needs JavaScript. The command in each card's "Verify the download" works without it.
download.verifier.mismatch_pasted: Does not match the checksum you pasted ({algo}).
download.verifier.invalid_pasted: The pasted value is not a SHA-256 or SHA-512 checksum (hex or base64), so it was not compared.
download.verifier.no_match: No match: the computed SHA-256 is
download.verifier.no_match_listed: It matches none of the checksums listed for this release.
download.verifier.too_large: {name} is larger than 1 GB, which is too large to check in the browser. Use the command shown in the card instead.
download.verifier.unsupported: This browser cannot compute checksums here (it needs a secure connection). Use the command shown in the card instead.
download.verifier.proves: A match shows that the file is exactly the one published for this release and was not corrupted or swapped on the way.
download.verifier.limits: It cannot replace the signature check that the app's updater does: the checksums here come from the same release page as the files.

report.title: Report a problem
report.lead: Something does not work as it should? Tell us on GitHub, where the people who build {brand} track every problem in the open.
report.check.search: Search the {linkHtml}. If the problem is already there, add what you know to that issue instead of opening a new one.
report.check.update: Update to the {linkHtml}: the problem may already be fixed.
report.check.one: One problem per report. Two problems in one report are hard to track.
report.check.private: Leave out anything private: no passwords, recovery keys, recovery codes, tokens or private messages, neither in the text nor in screenshots or logs.
report.check.public: Reports are public. Everyone can read them, and they stay on GitHub.
report.check.account: You need a GitHub account to report. Creating one is free.
report.cta_text: GitHub asks what the problem is about and then opens the form in the right place. The form says which details help.
report.discussions: Questions, help with a node, or an idea for a new feature? Ask in the {linkHtml}.
report.security_text: Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability. Report it privately on GitHub instead: only you and the maintainers can see the report, and we work on the fix together with you there.
report.security_list: Report privately in the repository of the affected part:
report.security.protocol: The protocol or the encryption design
report.security_policy: The {linkHtml} says what to include and what we promise.
report.info_title: Where to find the version and the logs
report.info_lead: Name the version and, if you can, add the messages the app or the node wrote. Read them first and remove anything private.
report.info.web: Name your browser and its version, and the address of your node. Error messages are in the browser's console: press F12 (on a Mac Cmd+Option+I) and open Console. The version of the official node is on the {linkHtml}.
report.info.desktop: Settings → App shows the app's version. The app writes no log file; on Linux, starting it from a terminal shows its messages there.
report.info.node: {logsHtml} shows the node's log, and {versionHtml} answers with its version. The log contains addresses and usernames: remove them before you post it.
